answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text: Including system wide impacts in decision-making is crucial to ensure that we spend our resources in a way that reduces emissions most efficiently and avoids greenwashing claims. Methods are already well-proven in practice and integrated in publicly available databases.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: It is not clear from the formula that the marginal emissions rate is the net emissions rate per MWh of the electricity project minus the emissions rate per marginal MWh of the baseline. This was clearer in the old text, although the sign was reversed, so that emission reductions had a positive sign and emissions a negative.

answers.label: Why secondary effects should be excluded
answers.text: It is preferable that secondary effects are included in scope 3, so that similar data and rules are applied to all similar activities in scope 3, whether electricity-related or not. We assume a similar delimitation of scope 2 would then be made in the GHG protocol’s inventory accounting standards.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: For reporting purposes, emission impacts should be reported annually on an ex-post basis. However, in a decision-making context, impacts should be assessed ex–ante over the full lifetime of the project to ensure that total lifetime emissions are properly considered in the decision.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Together, the required tests are sufficient and necessary to prove additionality, simple to perform based on available data, and the ones currently used to produce consequential (counterfactual) databases.

The optional tests give additional security.

The common practice test is inappropriate due to too many false positives and negatives.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text: The common practice test is inappropriate due to too many false positives and negatives.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text: At this stage, we do not have sufficient evidence to conclude which of the proposed operating margin methodologies is most appropriate. The suitability of operating margin methodologies should be determined based on empirical testing against historical data, assessing how accurately each method quantifies operating marginal emissions.

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text: Data may not always be available for all of the methods, so it is good to keep more options open, ideally presented as a hierarchy depending on data availability, where recent capacity additions would be a default that is always available although the scenario and expansion modelling methods would use more relevant data. Average emission rates are not relevant for a consequential model.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: Grid region is the most relevant for marginal data, and data can be estimated for all grids, as demonstrated by Watt-time

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Averaging over the year would be sufficient, but larger granularity useful.

answers.label: Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text:
Since there will be a time lag between an increase in electricity demand and the resulting deployment of new electricity generation capacity, this time lag can be used as weight for the operational marginal, relative to the weight for the build marginal, which should reflect the lifetime during which the newly built capacity would be operational. Since the lifetime of electricity generation assets generally largely exceeds the time lag between a change in demand and capacity expansion, the build margin can be expected to dominate the overall results in many cases. We suggest a default weighting factor for the operational:build marginal of 1:10, as an average across technologies. Project-specific weighting could be allowed when sufficient contextual information is available, although to avoid gaming, it may be preferable to use a fixed weighting factor.

A general comment is that these considerations are only valid for an increasing electricity market. For a decreasing electricity market, the build (decommissioning) and operating margin will be the same.
